description: We are a team passionate about space, engineering, and AI. We aim to build an interactive space mission design simulator where users can design spacecraft, select instruments, plan orbits, and balance real engineering constraints such as budget, mass, power, and communication. Our goal is to make space mission planning accessible, educational, and engaging through simulation and AI-powered optimization
summary:
Luminar Horizon is an interactive 3D browser game that turns space mission design into a hands-on engineering challenge. Players build a fictional wildfire-monitoring CubeSat, select its instruments, orbit, launch service, and ground stations, then operate it across three simulated days.

Every decision has consequences: a better camera can demand more power, fill storage faster, and overwhelm communications. Success depends on delivering useful observations to the ground on time—not simply collecting data. An explanatory mission report helps players identify bottlenecks, redesign their spacecraft, and compare results.

The project addresses the challenge by connecting spacecraft design, launch, orbital operations, and scientific outcomes in one playable experience. Real NASA FIRMS fire detections provide clearly labeled geographical context. Designed for students and curious learners, Luminar Horizon makes mission trade-offs visible and encourages learning through experimentation.
details:
Luminar Horizon, developed by ZagQ, lets players experience the complete design–operate–evaluate cycle of an educational space mission.

Its first scenario, Earth Guardian, challenges players to design a CubeSat for wildfire observation. In an interactive 3D hangar, players configure the spacecraft’s structure, payload, solar arrays, battery, communications, storage, and pointing system. They also choose an orbit, launch service, and ground stations. Engineering checks reveal whether the design meets its budget, mass, power, and launch constraints.

Players then simulate three mission days around a 3D Earth. The simulation connects orbital position and sunlight with battery charge, observation opportunities, storage, ground-station visibility, and data transmission. Scientific observations earn credit only when they meet the mission’s requirements and reach the ground before their deadline.

The mission report explains the outcome, allowing players to investigate failures and compare redesigned missions. Preset designs demonstrate different engineering approaches and bottlenecks. Browser saves and export/import features support continued experimentation.

Our creative approach is to make the entire journey of scientific data part of the game: from collecting an observation to storing it onboard and delivering it to its users. This demonstrates why a powerful instrument alone cannot guarantee a successful mission.

An optional NASA FIRMS overlay displays a dated sample of real NOAA-20 VIIRS fire detections. These observations are clearly separated from fictional mission targets and scoring. The published version uses a bundled dataset rather than a live feed.

We built the project using TypeScript, React, Next.js, Three.js, HTML/CSS, Blender, and Python, with Vitest and Playwright supporting verification. Development included AI assistance through Codex and Claude, directed and reviewed by the project team.

Design priorities included understandable feedback, reproducible results, browser performance, fullscreen visualization, keyboard and touch alternatives, and light and dark themes. Hardware specifications and simulation assumptions are intentionally simplified for education. The intended impact is to help learners understand how connected engineering decisions shape mission success.
